EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper wave dropping south across the Great Lakes and it's associated cold front brought widespread accumulating snow to the region New Year's Eve and into the new year across the ridges of western Pennsylvania and northern West Virginia. Enhanced orographic lift resulted in higher totals across the Laurel Highlands and eastern West Virginia ridges, with relatively high snow ratios between 18:1 and 21:1. Widespread Advisory level snow was also observed across the region, ranging from 2.5 inches to 5.5 inches outside of the ridges of Pennsylvania and West Virginia.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread snowfall, generally exceeding advisory criteria but falling short of warning criteria, fell across the county with amounts ranging from 3-4 inches and the highest total of 4.2 inches reported by the public 1 mile south of Follansbee.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of Arctic High pressure resided to the north prior to this storm leaving the region in an anomalously cold airmass. To the south, Gulf of America moisture was brought north by a robust southern jet stream. The intersection of these features resulted in a significant amount of wintry precipitation falling across the eastern Panhandle of West Virginia. This was a Miller B set-up, so warm air was brought north during the event resulting in sleet and freezing rain to mix in. In terms of accumulations, snowfall amounts (which include sleet) averaged 6 to 12. If you separate sleet, a general 2 to 5 inches were reported across the state. Freezing rain amounts of a trace to locally a tenth of an inch were observed as well. To capture the true magnitude of this event, the actual melted liquid with this storm was near 2 inches across the state. Sleet avalanches were reported across the mountains which buried roads with upwards of 10 feet of sleet closing them for days.

A snow squall crossed Mercer County during the morning hours to produce gusty winds, blowing snow, a sudden drop in temperature, and near whiteout conditions. The Bluefield ASOS measured a gust up to 37 mph with heavy snow, which caused the visibility to drop to under one quarter of a mile.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow Squall - A snow squall crossed the Bluefield airport, which the ASOS recorded a wind gust of 37 mph with heavy snow and the visibility under one quarter of a mile.  Key Impacts:  traffic delays, reduced visibility, blowing snow.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure passing through Ontario dragged a strong cold front west to east across the region in the afternoon hours. Boundary orthogonal bands of snow squalls developed ahead of the front with steep low level lapse rates and non-zero surface-based CAPE. The result was a widespread area of snow bands reducing visibility to a quarter mile or less with gusty wind greater than 35 mph and rapid accumulation on roadways resulting in at least one highway accident.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report of less than a quarter mile visibility and one inch of snow accumulation in a snow squall.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of low pressure developed across Texas and moved eastward towards the Appalachian Mountains, while Arctic high pressure also tracked eastward across the northern Plains and Great Lakes. The Arctic high reached the Appalachian Mountains first and wedged southward against the eastern slopes of the Blue Ridge to provide cold air near the surface. Meanwhile, the area of low pressure dissipated across the mountains, while a secondary area of low pressure formed off the North Carolina coast. This pattern set up a Miller B winter storm with the precipitation type as initially snow on January 24 but changing over to sleet and freezing rain by January 25 due to a substantial warm nose aloft. Notable impacts were documented during this winter storm in the form of transportation delays.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A wintry mix occurred with reports of up to 4.0 inches of snow, up to 2.7 inches of sleet, and up to 0.20 inches of freezing rain. Key Impacts: transportation delays.

A large area of strong low pressure tracked up the eastern seaboard downstream of a digging positive to neutrally tilted trough. Deep moisture through the dendritic growth zone and strong forcing resulted in widespread significant snowfall accumulation greater than 6 across the entire county warning area with amounts generally falling between 10-18. Localized amounts under narrow frontogenetically-forced bands reached up to 22 inches. An intruding mid-level warm nose reduced snow amounts slightly in northern West Virginia and resulted in a period of some mixing of snow with freezing rain and sleet.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A southern stream disturbance skirted across the Upper Mississippi Valley into the Carolinas beginning on January 30th, with the northern fringes of the disturbance extending into portions of southern West Virginia. Snow began in the coalfields around daybreak on the 30th and continued to snow for the next 24 hours as the storm tracked into the Mid-Atlantic region. Snow accumulations were mainly contained to Wyoming and McDowell Counties due to the southern trajectory of this event. Local Department of Highways measured around six inches of snow along the higher elevations of McDowell County and between two and three inches of snow in Wyoming County. All other counties in the state remained dry during this event.

A significant winter storm brought a mix of wintry precipitation to the area from the afternoon of January 24th into the 26th. Precipitation initially overspread the area as snow the evening of the 24th, then transitioned to a mix of snow, sleet, and freezing rain overnight into the morning of the 25th. Portions of northeast KY, southwest VA, and central and southern WV also experienced a period of rain as temperatures warmed slightly during the day. Temperatures plunged back below freezing in the wake of a cold front, with precipitation turning back to snow throughout the area that evening. Precipitation lingered overnight then tapered off the morning of the 26th.||Four to seven inches of snow accumulated across northern West Virginia and parts of the northeast mountains. Meanwhile, lesser amounts were observed across central and southern portions of the state where sleet, freezing rain, and even rain were more prevalent. Most counties reported at least a tenth or two of ice accumulation, though amounts ranged from a light glaze to over an inch across the area.  The highest ice amounts that were reported were an inch and a quarter in Nicholas County, just under an inch in Kanawha County, and just over three-quarters of an inch in Wayne County. In the mountains, significant sleet accumulations poured down the hillsides and created large piles that made several roadways impassable, primarily in Pocahontas County. Around an inch of sleet was also observed in parts of southeast West Virginia. With already saturated soils from earlier precipitation, and drains blocked by snow and ice, rain that fell across parts of southern West Virginia on the 25th led to isolated instances of flooding in Lincoln, Logan, and Cabell Counties.

Snow squalls moving through West Virginia on the morning of January 11th took place in the wake of a cold front that moved through earlier that day. These heavy bands of snow first began to impact portions of I-77 in Jackson and Roane Counties shortly after 8 o'clock in the morning, and continued to sweep through the state towards I-79 that morning. Obstructed surface visibilities were noted by traffic cameras and ASOS stations as squalls pressed through and were likely the cause of multiple traffic accidents that were reported that morning. Squalls quickly moved out of the forecast area before noon on the 11th.||In addition to the snow squalls tracking through the heart of the state, additional snow showers progressing into the West Virginia mountains prompted several inches in accumulations to fall on the 11th. Local Department of Highways measured between 2 to 5 inches of snow had fallen from southeast Randolph down into southeast Webster Counties. Strong winds accompanying these showers also resulted in a 47 mile per hour gust to be measured by a Mesonet station at Snowshoe on the afternoon of January 11th. Once this system departed, winds near the surface subsided.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple vehicle accidents occurred along I-79 in the midst of lowered visibility from the snow squall. Traffic webcams also captured the moments of obstructed visibility along the highway.

A strong Arctic outbreak settled into West Virginia for the second half of January. This was first initiated on January 20th in the wake of a cold front and a departing winter storm, followed by reinforcing shots of cold air through the last week of January. Most nights during this time featured Extreme Cold Warnings and Cold Weather Advisories in response to the dangerously cold wind chills. The first blast of cold air caused minimum wind chills of minus 10 to minus 26 along the northeast West Virginia mountains and minus 5 to minus 10 for the rest of the state. The final week of January featured areawide low temperatures below zero each morning, with even colder wind chills.

A significant winter storm brought a mix of wintry precipitation to the area from the afternoon of January 24th into the 26th. Precipitation initially overspread the area as snow the evening of the 24th, then transitioned to a mix of snow, sleet, and freezing rain overnight into the morning of the 25th. Portions of northeast KY, southwest VA, and central and southern WV also experienced a period of rain as temperatures warmed slightly during the day. Temperatures plunged back below freezing in the wake of a cold front, with precipitation turning back to snow throughout the area that evening. Precipitation lingered overnight then tapered off the morning of the 26th.||Four to seven inches of snow accumulated across northern West Virginia and parts of the northeast mountains. Meanwhile, lesser amounts were observed across central and southern portions of the state where sleet, freezing rain, and even rain were more prevalent. Most counties reported at least a tenth or two of ice accumulation, though amounts ranged from a light glaze to over an inch across the area.  The highest ice amounts that were reported were an inch and a quarter in Nicholas County, just under an inch in Kanawha County, and just over three-quarters of an inch in Wayne County. In the mountains, significant sleet accumulations poured down the hillsides and created large piles that made several roadways impassable, primarily in Pocahontas County. Around an inch of sleet was also observed in parts of southeast West Virginia. With already saturated soils from earlier precipitation, and drains blocked by snow and ice, rain that fell across parts of southern West Virginia on the 25th led to isolated instances of flooding in Lincoln, Logan, and Cabell Counties.

A significant winter storm brought a mix of wintry precipitation to the area from the afternoon of January 24th into the 26th. Precipitation initially overspread the area as snow the evening of the 24th, then transitioned to a mix of snow, sleet, and freezing rain overnight into the morning of the 25th. Portions of northeast KY, southwest VA, and central and southern WV also experienced a period of rain as temperatures warmed slightly during the day. Temperatures plunged back below freezing in the wake of a cold front, with precipitation turning back to snow throughout the area that evening. Precipitation lingered overnight then tapered off the morning of the 26th.||Four to seven inches of snow accumulated across northern West Virginia and parts of the northeast mountains. Meanwhile, lesser amounts were observed across central and southern portions of the state where sleet, freezing rain, and even rain were more prevalent. Most counties reported at least a tenth or two of ice accumulation, though amounts ranged from a light glaze to over an inch across the area.  The highest ice amounts that were reported were an inch and a quarter in Nicholas County, just under an inch in Kanawha County, and just over three-quarters of an inch in Wayne County. In the mountains, significant sleet accumulations poured down the hillsides and created large piles that made several roadways impassable, primarily in Pocahontas County. Around an inch of sleet was also observed in parts of southeast West Virginia. With already saturated soils from earlier precipitation, and drains blocked by snow and ice, rain that fell across parts of southern West Virginia on the 25th led to isolated instances of flooding in Lincoln, Logan, and Cabell Counties.

Snow squalls moving through West Virginia on the morning of January 11th took place in the wake of a cold front that moved through earlier that day. These heavy bands of snow first began to impact portions of I-77 in Jackson and Roane Counties shortly after 8 o'clock in the morning, and continued to sweep through the state towards I-79 that morning. Obstructed surface visibilities were noted by traffic cameras and ASOS stations as squalls pressed through and were likely the cause of multiple traffic accidents that were reported that morning. Squalls quickly moved out of the forecast area before noon on the 11th.||In addition to the snow squalls tracking through the heart of the state, additional snow showers progressing into the West Virginia mountains prompted several inches in accumulations to fall on the 11th. Local Department of Highways measured between 2 to 5 inches of snow had fallen from southeast Randolph down into southeast Webster Counties. Strong winds accompanying these showers also resulted in a 47 mile per hour gust to be measured by a Mesonet station at Snowshoe on the afternoon of January 11th. Once this system departed, winds near the surface subsided.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A vehicle crash occurred at the intersection of Reedyville Road and Ripley Road in Spencer during the time that surface visibility was obstructed by passing squalls.

These heavy bands of snow first began to impact portions of I-77 in Jackson and Roane Counties shortly after 8 o'clock in the morning, and continued to sweep through the state towards I-79 that morning. Obstructed surface visibilities were noted by traffic cameras and ASOS stations as squalls pressed through and were likely the cause of multiple traffic accidents that were reported that morning. Squalls quickly moved out of the forecast area before noon on the 11th.||In addition to the snow squalls tracking through the heart of the state, additional snow showers progressing into the West Virginia mountains prompted several inches in accumulations to fall on the 11th. Local Department of Highways measured between 2 to 5 inches of snow had fallen from southeast Randolph down into southeast Webster Counties. Strong winds accompanying these showers also resulted in a 47 mile per hour gust to be measured by a Mesonet station at Snowshoe on the afternoon of January 11th. Once this system departed, winds near the surface subsided.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Traffic cameras along I-77 in Fairplain and another located in downtown Ripley showed rapid drops in visibility as the snow squall passed overhead.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorms developed on the afternoon of March 7th during a period of record warmth. These storms formed a broken line of loosely organized convection west of the area that afternoon ahead of a cold frontal passage. While some of the storms proved to be severe in Ohio, the threat waned quickly as they progressed east of the Ohio River into West Virginia that evening. Strong wind gusts were still associated with storms as they swept through the state, which caused isolated tree damage in Wood, Ritchie, and Upshur Counties. Further deterioration of storms took place on the evening of the 7th due to the loss of daytime heating, bringing the severe threat to an end.

This transitioned rain to snow during the late afternoon of March 16th as a secondary area of low pressure developed. Moderate to heavy snow continued through the evening before transitioning to snow showers and squalls overnight. These continued intermittently through the daylight hours of March 17th. Total snow accumulations of two to six inches were observed, with a few favored higher ridges nearing eight inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A passing low pressure system brought wintry precipitation to West Virginia for the start of March. While the central lowlands observed very little snow amounts due to warm ground conditions, a combination of snow and freezing rain laid along the higher terrain of the Appalachian mountains from March 2nd to March 3rd. While temperatures remained near freezing from the morning to the 2nd into the overnight hours, a steady rise on March 3rd then caused lingering precipitation to changeover to rain for the rest of the day.

A front lifted into the area on the 3rd of March and then continued to ripple through the region over the next couple of days. Rain initially spread southwest to northeast across the area on the afternoon of the 3rd, then the focus of moderate to heavy rain became more confined to southeast Ohio and north central West Virginia during the evening and overnight hours. Another wave of showers pushed across the area after daybreak, however precipitation amounts were fairly light. A lull in precipitation occurred mid to late morning, then precipitation began streaming back into the area from the west during the afternoon.||In the first twenty-four hours of the event, precipitation amounts ranged from around half an inch to two inches across northern West Virginia. Meanwhile, amounts generally remained under an inch within the southern half of the state. Highest amounts were observed in a narrow swath across Wood, Jackson, Wirt, Ritchie, Calhoun, and Gilmer counties. Another one to two and a half inches of rain fell across portions of the state as additional rounds of rain, and some thunderstorms, traversed the area into the morning of the 6th. Rises on local creeks, streams, and smaller rivers primarily led to flooded roads in Wood, Gilmer, and Ritchie Counties on the 4th, then runoff prompted minor flooding to develop on the Tygart Valley River at Mill Creek the morning of the 6th. Flooding came to an end once precipitation tapered off during the day.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flooding observed on Stillwell Road and Pristine Pointe.

Late afternoon and evening thunderstorms developed along and ahead of a slowly southeastward sagging cold front. A surge of temperatures into the upper 70s with dew points in the mid 50s provided an unstable environment with 1000 J/kg of MUCAPE and strong 40-50 knot effective bulk shear. 500-600 J/kg of that CAPE was within the hail growth zone, and mid-level lapse rates were steep > 7 C/km. This supported severe thunderstorms with hail up to golf ball size and sporadic wind damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A tightened pressure gradient stemming from an advancing low pressure system resulted in a windy day across the state of West Virginia on March 13th. A slight uptick was noted in the morning, then later increasing to peak gusts of 45 to 55 miles per hour across the Central Appalachians as daytime heating helped mix down the stronger winds from aloft. Winds of this intensity prevailed into the late afternoon and evening hours before gradually declining around sunset that evening as the pressure gradient eased its hold over the area. Utility companies and county 911 call centers reported numerous downed trees and power lines across their respective counties as a result of these strong winds.

Winds of this intensity prevailed into the late afternoon and evening hours before gradually declining around sunset that evening as the pressure gradient eased its hold over the area. Utility companies and county 911 call centers reported numerous downed trees and power lines across their respective counties as a result of these strong winds.

A strong low pressure system that promoted strong to severe thunderstorms across West Virginia early in the day on March 16th quickly shifted gears into winter weather as a surge colder temperatures filtered into the region. Rain showers transitioned over to snow in the afternoon and evening and prevailed into the morning of March 17th. During that time, the bulk of the state received 2 to 4 inches of snow, while a narrow band of heavier snow transpired across north-central West Virginia. By the morning of the 17th, local CoCoRaHS and cooperative observers measured 5 to 8 inches of snow from Mason County and eastward over to Lewis County as a resulted of this heavy snow band. After a messy weather pattern from March 15th to the 17th, quieter conditions settled in under the guise of high pressure.

A strong cold front entered into West Virginia during the late night hours of March 15th and brought strong to severe thunderstorms through the state just before dawn on the 16th. Numerous areas of downed trees and power lines were observed across the area with this activity, then quickly followed by strong synoptic winds through the late morning hours. In the wake of the storms, weather stations in the state began to report gusts on the upwards of 40 miles per hour just before sunrise, with the strongest non-thunderstorm wind gust observed at the Huntington airport of 48 miles per hour. High pressure building in from the west later on the morning of March 16th alleviated the strong post-frontal winds across the state.

A tightened pressure gradient stemming from an advancing low pressure system resulted in a windy day across the state of West Virginia on March 13th. A slight uptick was noted in the morning, then later increasing to peak gusts of 45 to 55 miles per hour across the Central Appalachians as daytime heating helped mix down the stronger winds from aloft. Winds of this intensity prevailed into the late afternoon and evening hours before gradually declining around sunset that evening as the pressure gradient eased its hold over the area. Utility companies and county 911 call centers reported numerous downed trees and power lines across their respective counties as a result of these strong winds.

A strong cold front entered into West Virginia during the late night hours of March 15th and brought strong to severe thunderstorms through the state just before dawn on the 16th. Numerous areas of downed trees and power lines were observed across the area with this activity, then quickly followed by strong synoptic winds through the late morning hours. In the wake of the storms, weather stations in the state began to report gusts on the upwards of 40 miles per hour just before sunrise, with the strongest non-thunderstorm wind gust observed at the Huntington airport of 48 miles per hour. High pressure building in from the west later on the morning of March 16th alleviated the strong post-frontal winds across the state.

Very cold temperatures triumphing over West Virginia that began at the end of January spilled into the start February. Overnight low temperatures observed by cooperative observers and members of the CoCoRaHS program were in the single digits for the first two days of the month, with a few somewhat warmer nights before plummeting back down to dangerous temperatures and wind chills. Temperatures sprung back up above freezing on February 9th as a strong push of warmer air arrived from the southwest. However, the colder air remained entrenched across the higher elevations of the mountains until the morning of February 10th once the warmer air filtered up over the ridgetops. Daytime temperatures for the middle of the month hovered in the mid 50s to mid 60s for much of the lowlands and the mid 30s to mid 40s across the spine of the Appalachians, bringing the cold spell to an end.

A strong low pressure system brought one more strong burst of snow to West Virginia before the winter season began winding down from February 22nd to the 24th. As the storm arrived from the south, it received help from colder temperatures pressing down from the Great Lakes region. Unseasonably warm temperatures in the days leading up to this event allowed for initial precipitation to fall as rain for most locations before changing over to a wintry mix shortly after midnight on February 22nd. As temperatures continued to plummet down before freezing, precipitation changed fully over to snow. Intermittent breaks in snow showers continued for the next 24 hours, promoting significant snow accumulations along the spine of the Appalachians ranging between 12 to 20 inches along the westward facing ridgetops, while only 1 to 3 inches of snow fell in the West Virginia lowlands. The storm tracked to the east during the early morning hours of February 24th, bringing this winter event to an end.

A frontal boundary sank into the area on the 19th of February and then remained in the vicinity as a low-pressure system moved northeast into the Great Lakes region. The boundary became occluded overhead before being ushered northeast out of the area by the parent low on the 20th. Meanwhile, a cold front approached from the west and then washed out as it moved through the middle Ohio Valley later in the day. The first round of precipitation lifted north across West Virginia the morning of the 19th, then rounds of more robust showers and thunderstorms rolled through the area that afternoon into the night. After a very brief break in activity, more showers and storms spread into the area from the southwest shortly after midnight and then slid east across the mountains by mid-morning on the 20th. Drier conditions then took hold for the rest of the day.||Strong to severe storms downed multiple trees and power lines, and produced hail between one and one-and-three-quarter inches in size. While rainfall amounts of two inches or less were observed across much of the area, portions of the southern coal fields received two to three and a half inches. Excessive rainfall caused flooding on some roads as local creeks, streams, and smaller rivers exceeded their banks in Boone and Logan Counties. A combination of rainfall and snowmelt also prompted minor flooding on Mill Creek in Randolph County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree fell into power lines and blocked Little Oak Street in Williamson.

However, the colder air remained entrenched across the higher elevations of the mountains until the morning of February 10th once the warmer air filtered up over the ridgetops. Daytime temperatures for the middle of the month hovered in the mid 50s to mid 60s for much of the lowlands and the mid 30s to mid 40s across the spine of the Appalachians, bringing the cold spell to an end.

A strong low pressure system brought one more strong burst of snow to West Virginia before the winter season began winding down from February 22nd to the 24th. As the storm arrived from the south, it received help from colder temperatures pressing down from the Great Lakes region. Unseasonably warm temperatures in the days leading up to this event allowed for initial precipitation to fall as rain for most locations before changing over to a wintry mix shortly after midnight on February 22nd. As temperatures continued to plummet down before freezing, precipitation changed fully over to snow. Intermittent breaks in snow showers continued for the next 24 hours, promoting significant snow accumulations along the spine of the Appalachians ranging between 12 to 20 inches along the westward facing ridgetops, while only 1 to 3 inches of snow fell in the West Virginia lowlands. The storm tracked to the east during the early morning hours of February 24th, bringing this winter event to an end.

A frontal boundary sank into the area on the 19th of February and then remained in the vicinity as a low-pressure system moved northeast into the Great Lakes region. The boundary became occluded overhead before being ushered northeast out of the area by the parent low on the 20th. Meanwhile, a cold front approached from the west and then washed out as it moved through the middle Ohio Valley later in the day. The first round of precipitation lifted north across West Virginia the morning of the 19th, then rounds of more robust showers and thunderstorms rolled through the area that afternoon into the night. After a very brief break in activity, more showers and storms spread into the area from the southwest shortly after midnight and then slid east across the mountains by mid-morning on the 20th. Drier conditions then took hold for the rest of the day.||Strong to severe storms downed multiple trees and power lines, and produced hail between one and one-and-three-quarter inches in size. While rainfall amounts of two inches or less were observed across much of the area, portions of the southern coal fields received two to three and a half inches. Excessive rainfall caused flooding on some roads as local creeks, streams, and smaller rivers exceeded their banks in Boone and Logan Counties. A combination of rainfall and snowmelt also prompted minor flooding on Mill Creek in Randolph County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: High water was observed on WV Route 85.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: In the wake of a cold front on the morning of February 20th, gusty to strong post-frontal wind gusts took hold across West Virginia. This was due to a tightened pressure gradient that formed overhead, creating strong winds aloft that were capable of mixing down to the surface. This resulted in observed wind gusts on the order of 45 to 57 miles per hour across the state, which caused downed trees and power lines in many West Virginia counties. Impacts from the strong winds waned by the late evening hours on the 20th as high pressure encroached from the west.

An upper low over the region produced scattered snow showers across the region but relatively limited forcing resulted in only and inch or two in the lowlands, mainly on elevated and grassy surfaces.  However. the ridges of WV saw much higher snow rates due to forcing due to orographic lift.|||||||Clipper tracking over the Great Lakes resulted in light fluffy snow with snow-to-liquid ratios ranging from 18:1 to 21:1. Snow amounts generally ranged from 1 to 2 inches in the lowlands, but the observed amounts in the ridges West Virginia were much higher.  The highest observed was 16 inches near Red Creek in Tucker County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread snowfall fell across Preston county. The highest reported amount was 11 inches near Kingwood.

Robust bands of snow tracked through the state of West Virginia from February 6th to the 7th, leading to snow amounts ranging from 3 to 6 inches along the mountains and 1 to 3 inches in the lower elevations. A frontal passage that occurred during this event also led to a brief stint of strong surface wind gusts ranging from 35 to 52 miles per hour. Behind the front, additional snow squalls and dangerous cold filtered into the Central Appalachians. High pressure shifting in from the west allowed for snow showers to taper off quickly after sunrise on February 7th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system brought one more strong burst of snow to West Virginia before the winter season began winding down from February 22nd to the 24th. As the storm arrived from the south, it received help from colder temperatures pressing down from the Great Lakes region. The storm tracked to the east during the early morning hours of February 24th, bringing this winter event to an end.

Meanwhile, a cold front approached from the west and then washed out as it moved through the middle Ohio Valley later in the day. The first round of precipitation lifted north across West Virginia the morning of the 19th, then rounds of more robust showers and thunderstorms rolled through the area that afternoon into the night. After a very brief break in activity, more showers and storms spread into the area from the southwest shortly after midnight and then slid east across the mountains by mid-morning on the 20th. Drier conditions then took hold for the rest of the day.||Strong to severe storms downed multiple trees and power lines, and produced hail between one and one-and-three-quarter inches in size. While rainfall amounts of two inches or less were observed across much of the area, portions of the southern coal fields received two to three and a half inches. Excessive rainfall caused flooding on some roads as local creeks, streams, and smaller rivers exceeded their banks in Boone and Logan Counties. A combination of rainfall and snowmelt also prompted minor flooding on Mill Creek in Randolph County.

Very cold temperatures triumphing over West Virginia that began at the end of January spilled into the start February. Overnight low temperatures observed by cooperative observers and members of the CoCoRaHS program were in the single digits for the first two days of the month, with a few somewhat warmer nights before plummeting back down to dangerous temperatures and wind chills. Temperatures sprung back up above freezing on February 9th as a strong push of warmer air arrived from the southwest. However, the colder air remained entrenched across the higher elevations of the mountains until the morning of February 10th once the warmer air filtered up over the ridgetops. Daytime temperatures for the middle of the month hovered in the mid 50s to mid 60s for much of the lowlands and the mid 30s to mid 40s across the spine of the Appalachians, bringing the cold spell to an end.

A strong low pressure system brought one more strong burst of snow to West Virginia before the winter season began winding down from February 22nd to the 24th. As the storm arrived from the south, it received help from colder temperatures pressing down from the Great Lakes region. Unseasonably warm temperatures in the days leading up to this event allowed for initial precipitation to fall as rain for most locations before changing over to a wintry mix shortly after midnight on February 22nd. As temperatures continued to plummet down before freezing, precipitation changed fully over to snow. Intermittent breaks in snow showers continued for the next 24 hours, promoting significant snow accumulations along the spine of the Appalachians ranging between 12 to 20 inches along the westward facing ridgetops, while only 1 to 3 inches of snow fell in the West Virginia lowlands. The storm tracked to the east during the early morning hours of February 24th, bringing this winter event to an end.

An Alberta Clipper brought a period of moderate snow during the afternoon and early evening hours of February 6th. This tapered to light snow through the evening. Between 11 PM February 6th and 2 AM February 7th, a potent snow squall moved through along an Arctic Front. This reduced visibilities below one quarter of a mile, wind gusts to 50 mph, and quick accumulations near 1-2 in about 30 minutes. By the time the snow ended, total accumulations of 4 to 7 were observed. Winds gusted to 50 mph through the day of February 7th resulting in significant blowing and drifting of snow. Several roads were reported drifted shut.

A strong Nor'Easter moved northward along the Eastern Seaboard February 22nd into the 23rd. Temperatures were marginal to start outside of elevation, making the snowfall totals elevation dependent. By the end of the event, snowfall totals of 6 to 15 inches were observed across western Pendleton and western Grant Counties with lesser amounts of 3 to 6 inches across western Mineral. Further east across the eastern panhandle, totals were elevation dependent with the ridges observing 2 to 4 inches and the valleys observing a coating to 2 inches.

In the wake of a cold front on the morning of February 20th, gusty to strong post-frontal wind gusts took hold across West Virginia. This was due to a tightened pressure gradient that formed overhead, creating strong winds aloft that were capable of mixing down to the surface. This resulted in observed wind gusts on the order of 45 to 57 miles per hour across the state, which caused downed trees and power lines in many West Virginia counties. Impacts from the strong winds waned by the late evening hours on the 20th as high pressure encroached from the west.
